narrative:
The model estimated an 85.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and that high-risk estimate is why your law school application was denied. This does not mean the decision is a final judgment about your ability; it means the model found your academic profile closely resembled students who struggled on the bar exam.

The strongest factor pushing toward failure was your third-year class-standing decile. Your value was 1.00, while admitted students averaged near 6, and this was the single most influential issue in the prediction. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 22, which is well below the admitted-student average of about 37 and strongly increased the predicted risk of failure. The third factor was your first-year class-standing decile, also 1.00 versus an admitted average near 6; it pushed toward failure as well, though less strongly than your third-year standing.

To improve a future application, focus on concrete evidence that reduces bar-exam risk. Retake the LSAT after structured preparation, seek academic advising about your class standing and any available grade-improvement options, and consider delaying reapplication until you can show stronger academic performance or additional legal-study preparation. Ask admissions staff what they would need to see changed, and consider schools or programs where your current profile is a better fit.
